description: We’re Mirrix, a team of four from Tashkent taking on the Martian Map challenge: one interactive map of Mars that combines NASA mission data so you can plan a safe walk and spot science worth studying. We care about clean design and a working demo. We have two spots open and want someone with maps/GIS or satellite data experience, a designer, or anyone with a space science background. If you’re curious about Mars and ready for 48 hours of work, message us.
summary: ARES Navigator is Team Mirrix’s interactive Marswalk planner. It combines NASA and USGS imagery, elevation, and infrared data with a Mars solar clock. Users can explore Mars in 3D, compare routes through Jezero Crater, check whether a traverse fits within daylight, and rehearse science stops in Field mode.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
ARES Navigator lets users plan a hypothetical astronaut traverse from start to finish. The Jezero demo opens the western fan on a 3D terrain model and loads three proposed stops for comparing sediment layers. Users can switch between visible-light imagery, elevation, and historical daytime infrared imagery. An A* pathfinding algorithm uses the elevation grid and a user-defined slope limit to generate route options. The app compares distance, slope, estimated travel time, and science stops. Users can then check the daylight window, simulate the walk in Field mode, record observations, and export a JSON or print-ready report.

What benefits does it have?
It makes route trade-offs visible. In our Jezero demo, the shortest route covers 2.95 km and reaches a maximum modeled slope of 14.7°. The gentler route adds about 120 m and lowers that slope to 8.7°, while reaching the same three science stops. The map, elevation profile, and report help users explain which route they chose and why.

What is the intended impact?
We want students, educators, and early-stage mission designers to use real planetary data to make decisions they can explain and reproduce. ARES Navigator is an educational and research prototype. Operational astronaut planning would require validated local hazard, weather, and crew-performance data.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use?
We developed the app on Windows laptops using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. WebGL renders the globe and 3D terrain, Canvas renders the 2D map, and Web Workers handle routing and terrain processing. We used Python to prepare scientific data, Node.js and Playwright for testing, Git and GitHub Pages for publication, and Codex to assist with development.

How is the project creative?
A shared Mars clock connects the Sun’s position, the map lighting, the route timeline, and the simulated astronaut’s progress. A user can keep the same route and change only the departure time to see how daylight affects the plan. On the demo sol, a 17:30 local solar time start puts part of the traverse after sunset. The Best window tool suggests 11:07 for the same route and daylight reserve.

What factors did we consider?
We considered terrain resolution, slope limits, walking speed, equipment reserves, time spent at science stops, and daylight before sunset. The 20 m elevation grid can show larger terrain features and slopes, while individual rocks and smaller obstacles require finer observations. Walking times and daylight margins are modeled estimates. The THEMIS layer shows historical infrared brightness, and the Perseverance photos provide regional context for the proposed stops.
